newsitem.title: USA: Clinton appointee pushed deal for donor - NY Times.
newsitem.headline: Clinton appointee pushed deal for donor - NY Times.

text.p: An appointee of President Bill Clinton's at the Export-Import Bank tried last year to push through an unusual $6.5 million financing deal sought by a Thai woman whose large donations to the Democratic Party are under investigation, The New York Times reported on Thursday.

Citing interviews and government records, the Times reported in a Washington-datelined story that the deal was pushed by Maria Haley, who had been a long-time aide to Clinton before her appointment at the bank.
The proposed deal called for the government bank to help a company controlled by one of Thailand's wealthiest families to finance a Blockbuster video store franchise in Bangkok, the Times said.

The newspaper reported officials of the bank said the proposal initially ran into stiff resistance because it seemed to fall outside the mandate of the institution, which is to provide low-cost government financing to encourage exports and thereby support jobs in America.

But Haley, who by then had become one of the bank's directors, prodded its staff to support the project, the Times said. The deal won approval from one group of bank officials before collapsing amid unresolved questions about the franchise's operations, it said.

The newspaper said the project was put together in large part by Pauline Kanchanalak, a Thai businesswoman living in Virginia who attended an important meeting of Export-Import Bank officials at Haley's office last summer. The Times said records showed Kanchanalak and relatives gave more than $200,000 to the Democratic Party, most of which was returned because of questions about its origins.

The Times said it was unclear if Haley knew of Kanchanalak's donations, and quoted a White House spokesman as saying Clinton was not aware of the Blockbuster deal, which would have been a small one for the bank.

The Times said Haley's effort to push the deal was one of the first signs that some Democratic donors with foreign ties sought more specific help from the government than coffee meetings and photos with Clinton.

Kanchanalak's donations were solicited by John Huang, the Democratic Party fundraiser now at the center of federal probes into questionable donations from Asian and Asian-American business interests, the Times said. It reported that Huang arranged for Kanchanalak to attend a White House coffee meeting with Clinton last June 18, a day when she made $85,000 of the contributions to the party.

Bank records showed Huang called Haley on June 18, and called her twice during a week in August when the Blockbuster deal's fate was being decided, the Times said. Huang and Haley had been friends since the mid-1980s in Little Rock, Arkansas, when they both knew then-Gov. Clinton, it said.

The Times said Haley was one of the first staff members hired by Clinton after he became governor in 1979. She later accompanied him on trade missions to Asia, heading the state's efforts to attract foreign investment, and after Clinton became president served as a deputy White House personnel director under Bruce Lindsey. She was nominated to the bank's board in 1994, it said.

Neither Haley nor Kanchanalak would comment on the Blockbuster deal, the Times said, and Huang and his lawyer have declined since last fall, when he first came under investigation, to talk about any aspect of his fundraising.

David Carter, the Export-Import Bank's vice president for communications, said he could not discuss specific deals but said "I am confident that the bank and Director Haley have acted appropriately at every turn."

The Times said a Thai conglomerate, the Sun Tech Group, controlled by one of Thailand's wealthiest businessmen, Sawasdi Horrungruang, approached the Ex-Im Bank about the deal in late 1995 or early 1996.

One of Sun Tech's subsidiaries had agreed to pay $7.7 million to the Blockbuster Entertainment Group, a unit of Viacom Inc, for the rights to operate 100 video rental stores in Thailand, it said. The deal was to be financed by SunTrust Credit, a Little Rock unit of a large Florida bank chain.
The Times said SunTrust asked the Ex-Im Bank to insure repayment of 85 percent of the loan, or $6.5 million.

Businessmen said the Thais sought help because financing for American-style franchise rights was hard to come by in Thailand, and a repayment guarantee from the bank would lower the interest rates they had to pay, the Times said.
